book-1-105.explanation: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria involves a biphasic IgG antibody: it binds and fixes complement in the cold, then hemolysis occurs on warming. Its usual target is the P antigen.
optionExplanations: ABO antigens are not the usual target of this particular autoantibody.
I specificity is more typical of cold agglutinin disease.
P specificity is characteristic of the Donath-Landsteiner antibody.
Rh-associated specificity is more typical of many warm autoantibodies.

quickCheck.question: Does the Donath-Landsteiner reaction require cold binding followed by warming?

book-1-106.questionInPlainEnglish: Which deficiency best explains very large red cells plus numbness and trouble walking?
book-1-106.explanation: B12 is needed both for normal DNA synthesis and nervous-system function. Deficiency can therefore cause megaloblastic anemia together with numbness, poor balance, or difficulty walking. Folate deficiency can mimic the blood picture but usually lacks this neurologic pattern.
optionExplanations: Folate deficiency can cause megaloblastic anemia but does not explain the characteristic neurologic findings as well.
Vitamin B12 deficiency fits both macrocytic anemia and nerve symptoms.
Vitamin B6 deficiency can impair heme synthesis, usually producing a different anemia pattern.
Vitamin C deficiency causes collagen-related bleeding rather than this combined blood and nerve picture.
book-1-106.memory: Big red cells plus numb feet: think B12.

quickCheck.question: Which deficiency causes megaloblastic anemia with possible neurologic damage?

book-1-106.sourceNote: The smear reference is Color Plate 11; the clinical neurologic clue is independently useful.

book-1-107.questionInPlainEnglish: Which blood test is most likely abnormal when red-cell granules stain positively for iron?
book-1-107.explanation: Prussian blue confirms that the granules contain iron, identifying siderotic inclusions such as Pappenheimer bodies. Iron loading can raise serum ferritin, the storage-iron marker.
optionExplanations: Plasma hemoglobin reflects intravascular hemolysis rather than specifically identifying iron storage.
Serum ferritin can be elevated when these granules reflect iron overload.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies hemoglobin variants, not iron granules.
Parietal-cell antibodies investigate autoimmune B12 malabsorption rather than this iron finding.
book-1-107.memory: Prussian blue proves iron; ferritin reflects the warehouse.

quickCheck.question: What stain confirms that Pappenheimer bodies contain iron?

book-1-107.sourceNote: Iron inclusions can also occur after splenectomy without generalized iron overload; the book intends an iron-loading context.

book-1-108.explanation: A structural hemoglobinopathy changes the amino-acid sequence of a globin chain. The factory makes an altered version of the protein, as in Hb S or Hb C, rather than simply making too little of a normal chain.
optionExplanations: Reduced globin-chain quantity describes thalassemia.
Some variants affect oxygen handling, but complete inability to transport oxygen is not the definition.
Problems adding iron to heme concern heme synthesis rather than globin structure.
Production of structurally abnormal hemoglobin variants is the defining feature here.
book-1-108.memory: Hemoglobin variant changes quality; thalassemia changes quantity.

quickCheck.question: Is Hb S a structural variant or merely reduced chain production?

book-1-108.sourceNote: Hemoglobinopathy is sometimes used broadly to include thalassemias; this question uses the narrower structural-variant meaning.

book-1-109.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about hereditary spherocytosis is true?
book-1-109.explanation: An inherited membrane-skeleton defect causes red cells to lose membrane during circulation, especially through the spleen. They become dense spheres that cannot squeeze through splenic passages well and are trapped.
optionExplanations: The classic spherical appearance develops as defective cells lose membrane in circulation, not simply as the final shape made in marrow.
MCHC may rise because the cells are dense; a low MCHC is not typical.
Membrane loss and splenic trapping correctly describe the disease process.
Osmotic fragility is usually increased because reduced membrane reserve makes swelling harder to tolerate.
book-1-109.memory: Spherocytes lose surface, become spheres, and stick in the spleen.

quickCheck.question: Why do spherocytes have increased osmotic fragility?
quickCheck.answer: They have less spare membrane surface to accommodate swelling.

book-1-111.questionInPlainEnglish: Which condition does NOT usually cause anemia through chronic inflammation?
book-1-111.explanation: Chronic gastrointestinal blood loss removes iron from the body, leading mainly to iron-deficiency anemia. Anemia of chronic disease instead involves inflammatory iron trapping and a reduced production response.
optionExplanations: Persistent infections can generate chronic inflammatory signals and this anemia.
Noninfectious inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis, commonly causes it.
Chronic gastrointestinal bleeding mainly causes iron loss and is the exception.
Malignancy can cause inflammatory anemia, although it can produce anemia by other mechanisms too.
book-1-111.memory: Inflammation hides iron; bleeding loses iron.

quickCheck.question: What anemia is classically caused by chronic gastrointestinal bleeding?

book-1-112.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about Hb C DISEASE is FALSE?
book-1-112.explanation: Hb C disease means the person has two Hb C alleles. There is little or no Hb A and a large majority of Hb C. A pattern of about 60% A and 40% C describes Hb C trait instead.
optionExplanations: A 60% A/40% C pattern describes trait, so it is false for homozygous disease.
Target cells are common in Hb C disease; this is true.
Bar-shaped intracellular Hb C crystals may be present; this is true.
Hb C disease is usually milder than Hb SS disease; this is true.
book-1-112.memory: C trait keeps A; CC disease has mostly C.

quickCheck.question: Which condition typically retains more Hb A than Hb C: trait or disease?

book-1-113.questionInPlainEnglish: Which effect is characteristic of sickled red cells?
book-1-113.explanation: When deoxygenated Hb S forms fibers, red cells become stiff. They can block small vessels, reducing blood supply and causing painful ischemic injury.
optionExplanations: Low rather than high oxygen tension promotes sickling.
Sickled cells are mechanically vulnerable rather than unusually resistant to damage.
Sickling decreases flexibility, so increased deformability is incorrect.
Vessel obstruction by stiff sickled cells is a central feature.
book-1-113.memory: Sickle fibers stiffen cells and stop flow.

quickCheck.question: Why can sickling cause pain?
quickCheck.answer: Blocked vessels reduce oxygen delivery to tissues.

book-1-114.questionInPlainEnglish: Which anemia can retain a normal M:E ratio despite a very sparse marrow?
book-1-114.explanation: In aplastic anemia, both myeloid and erythroid production can fall together. Their ratio may stay normal even though the total amount of blood-making tissue is greatly reduced. A ratio measures balance, not total activity.
optionExplanations: Sickle hemolysis usually expands erythroid precursors and lowers the M:E ratio.
Aplastic anemia may reduce both lineages proportionally, preserving a ratio near 4:1.
Beta-thalassemia major strongly expands erythroid precursors and lowers the ratio.
Megaloblastic anemia usually produces erythroid hyperplasia and a reduced ratio.
book-1-114.memory: A normal ratio can hide an almost empty factory.

quickCheck.question: Can normal M:E proportions prove normal overall marrow production?
quickCheck.answer: No; cellularity must also be assessed.

book-1-114.sourceNote: The ratio in aplastic anemia is variable and is not diagnostic by itself.

book-1-115.questionInPlainEnglish: What immune hemolysis best fits new spherocytes and jaundice in a patient with CLL?
book-1-115.explanation: CLL can disrupt immune control and trigger warm autoimmune hemolysis. Macrophages remove parts of antibody-coated membranes, forming spherocytes. Because an underlying disease is known, this is secondary rather than idiopathic.
optionExplanations: Idiopathic warm hemolysis has no identified associated cause; this patient has CLL.
Secondary warm autoimmune hemolysis fits both the spherocytes and known CLL association.
Primary cold disease more often produces cold-related agglutination rather than this warm pattern.
PCH is a biphasic anti-P hemolysis, not the most likely CLL-associated pattern.
book-1-115.memory: CLL plus new spherocytic hemolysis suggests secondary warm AIHA.

quickCheck.question: Why is this warm autoimmune hemolysis called secondary?
quickCheck.answer: It is associated with an underlying disorder, CLL.

book-1-116.questionInPlainEnglish: Which finding would NOT support pernicious anemia?
book-1-116.explanation: Pernicious anemia blocks B12 absorption because intrinsic factor is missing or blocked. Without B12, DNA maturation lags behind cytoplasmic growth, producing megaloblastic rather than normal normoblastic marrow maturation.
optionExplanations: Gastric atrophy and low acid fit autoimmune loss of parietal cells.
Large oval cells and nuclear remnants can occur with megaloblastic anemia.
Normal normoblastic precursor maturation contradicts the expected megaloblastic process.
High LDH and bilirubin fit destruction of ineffective developing cells.
book-1-116.memory: Pernicious anemia: intrinsic factor fails, B12 falls, nuclei lag.

quickCheck.question: What type of marrow maturation is expected in untreated pernicious anemia?

book-1-117.questionInPlainEnglish: Which hemoglobin can migrate with Hb S but give a negative sickle solubility test?
book-1-117.explanation: Hb D can occupy the Hb S position on alkaline electrophoresis without behaving like Hb S in the solubility test. The negative solubility result therefore helps distinguish a co-migrating variant from sickling hemoglobin.
optionExplanations: Hb C migrates in a different alkaline group rather than the S position.
Hb D can co-migrate with S and remains soluble, fitting the pattern.
Hb E typically migrates with the C/A2 region rather than S.
Hb S should ordinarily give a positive solubility test at a 95% concentration.
book-1-117.memory: Same electrophoresis lane does not always mean same hemoglobin.

quickCheck.question: Which additional result argues against Hb S in this case?

book-1-117.sourceNote: Confirmatory hemoglobin methods are needed because electrophoretic co-migration is not unique to Hb D.

book-1-118.questionInPlainEnglish: Which enzyme deficiency can cause hemolysis after primaquine?
book-1-118.explanation: Primaquine can create oxidant stress. G6PD-deficient red cells cannot maintain enough reduced glutathione to protect hemoglobin, so hemoglobin denatures and the cells break down.
optionExplanations: Pyruvate kinase deficiency reduces ATP, but is not the classic primaquine-sensitive defect.
G6PD deficiency causes vulnerability to oxidant drugs such as primaquine.
2,3-BPG affects oxygen release rather than the main antioxidant defense.
Methemoglobin reductase deficiency mainly causes methemoglobinemia, not this classic drug-triggered hemolysis.
book-1-118.memory: Primaquine can expose a G6PD protection gap.

quickCheck.question: What red-cell defense is weakened in G6PD deficiency?

book-1-119.questionInPlainEnglish: Which acquired membrane disorder makes blood cells vulnerable to complement?
book-1-119.explanation: PNH arises from an acquired stem-cell mutation that prevents normal anchoring of protective surface proteins. Without defenses such as CD55 and CD59, complement can attack and lyse the cells.
optionExplanations: March hemoglobinuria is mechanical injury from repeated impact, such as running.
PNH is an acquired loss of complement-protective membrane proteins.
PCH is caused by a cold-reacting antibody rather than this acquired membrane-anchor defect.
Methemoglobinemia changes hemoglobin iron rather than complement protection.
book-1-119.memory: PNH loses CD55/CD59 shields against complement.

quickCheck.question: What modern laboratory method detects PNH cell populations?
quickCheck.answer: Flow cytometry for deficient GPI-linked markers.

book-1-119.sourceNote: The source wording about increased complement binding is imprecise; loss of complement regulation is the key mechanism. Older sucrose and Ham tests have been replaced by flow cytometry.

book-1-120.questionInPlainEnglish: Which drug or exposure is NOT a typical cause of reversible sideroblastic anemia?
book-1-120.explanation: Methotrexate blocks folate metabolism and therefore impairs DNA synthesis, producing megaloblastic changes. Lead, alcohol, and isoniazid can interfere with heme synthesis and cause acquired sideroblastic anemia.
optionExplanations: Methotrexate mainly causes antifolate megaloblastic changes, making it the exception.
Lead inhibits heme-production enzymes and can cause sideroblastic changes.
Isoniazid interferes with vitamin B6, which is required in heme synthesis.
Alcohol can impair heme synthesis and produce reversible sideroblastic changes.
book-1-120.memory: Methotrexate targets folate and DNA; isoniazid targets B6 and heme.

quickCheck.question: Which vitamin-related pathway does methotrexate inhibit?

book-1-121.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about normal dilutional anemia of pregnancy is FALSE?
book-1-121.explanation: During pregnancy, red-cell mass increases, but plasma volume increases even more. The red cells are diluted, so hemoglobin concentration falls without a true reduction in total red-cell number.
optionExplanations: A reduction in total erythrocyte number is false for normal dilutional pregnancy anemia.
Normal size and hemoglobin content of individual cells fit dilutional anemia.
Normal pregnancy-related dilution does not itself imply a fetal oxygen deficit.
Increased plasma volume is the reason for the relative anemia.
book-1-121.memory: Pregnancy adds red cells, but adds even more plasma.

quickCheck.question: Why can hemoglobin concentration fall while total red-cell mass rises?
quickCheck.answer: Plasma volume rises by a larger proportion.

book-1-122.questionInPlainEnglish: Why does chronic kidney failure commonly cause anemia?
book-1-122.explanation: The kidneys normally release EPO to stimulate red-cell production. Damaged kidneys produce too little of this signal, so marrow makes fewer red cells despite the body’s need for oxygen.
optionExplanations: Reduced EPO synthesis is the main mechanism emphasized here.
Cells still need oxygen; the problem is inadequate signaling, not absent demand.
Poor iron handling can contribute but does not explain the main kidney-specific mechanism.
Uremia can shorten red-cell survival, but inadequate EPO is the major cause listed.
book-1-122.memory: Failing kidneys send too little EPO mail to marrow.

quickCheck.question: Which hormone deficiency is central to renal anemia?

book-1-123.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about aplastic anemia is FALSE?
book-1-123.explanation: Aplastic anemia is mainly a failure to produce blood cells. Too few neutrophils cause infection risk, and too few platelets cause bleeding. Shortened red-cell survival is not its defining problem.
optionExplanations: Stem-cell dysfunction can produce aplastic marrow failure; this is true.
Severe neutropenia creates a life-threatening infection risk; this is true.
Thrombocytopenia can cause frequent bleeding; this is true.
Reduced red-cell survival describes destruction rather than the principal production failure and is the false statement.
book-1-123.memory: Aplasia reduces production, not primarily red-cell lifespan.

quickCheck.question: Which missing cell type drives infection risk in aplastic anemia?

book-1-124.questionInPlainEnglish: What type of anemia can the fish tapeworm cause?
book-1-124.explanation: The fish tapeworm can consume vitamin B12 in the intestine. If the host becomes B12-deficient, impaired DNA synthesis produces megaloblastic, usually macrocytic anemia.
optionExplanations: Microcytic anemia is more typical of iron loss, such as with hookworm.
Macrocytic anemia fits B12 depletion caused by the fish tapeworm.
Hemolytic anemia means accelerated destruction and is not the usual mechanism here.
Reduced effective production occurs, but the specific expected classification is macrocytic megaloblastic anemia.
book-1-124.memory: Fish tapeworm takes B12 and leaves big cells.

quickCheck.question: Which nutrient can Diphyllobothrium latum deprive its host of?

book-1-125.questionInPlainEnglish: In which condition is high EPO an inappropriate excess rather than compensation for low oxygen?
book-1-125.explanation: A renal tumor can produce EPO without a genuine oxygen shortage. Smoking and heart or lung disease may reduce effective oxygen delivery, so increased EPO in those settings can be compensatory.
optionExplanations: Renal tumors can release EPO inappropriately, causing secondary erythrocytosis.
Heavy smoking can impair oxygen delivery, prompting a compensatory EPO response.
Cardiovascular disease can reduce oxygen delivery and stimulate compensatory EPO.
Pulmonary disease can reduce oxygen uptake and stimulate compensatory EPO.
book-1-125.memory: Renal tumor EPO can be an unwanted signal, not an oxygen rescue.

quickCheck.question: What major hemoglobin derivative contributes to smoking-related tissue hypoxia?

book-1-125.sourceNote: The source incorrectly emphasizes methemoglobin in heavy smokers; carbon monoxide and carboxyhemoglobin are the usual explanation.

book-1-126.explanation: Thalassemia means the body makes too little of one globin-chain type. The chains may have a normal structure, but their quantities are unbalanced, leaving excess partner chains that damage red cells.
optionExplanations: A heme structural defect is not the defining thalassemia problem.
Reduced quantity of globin-chain synthesis defines thalassemia.
A qualitative chain-structure defect describes a structural hemoglobin variant.
Altered solubility characterizes some variants, especially Hb S, rather than defining thalassemia.
book-1-126.memory: Thalassemia is a quantity problem: too few chains.

quickCheck.question: In beta-thalassemia, is beta-chain quantity or alpha-chain quantity primarily reduced?

book-1-127.questionInPlainEnglish: Which combination of iron tests fits iron-deficiency anemia?
book-1-127.explanation: Iron stores fall, so ferritin is low. The liver makes more transferrin to collect scarce iron, but few binding sites are filled; therefore transferrin rises while its percentage saturation falls.
optionExplanations: Normal ferritin does not fit uncomplicated established iron-deficiency anemia as well as low ferritin.
Low transferrin is more characteristic of inflammation than uncomplicated iron deficiency.
High transferrin, low saturation, and low ferritin is the classic iron-deficiency combination.
High saturation contradicts the scarcity of circulating iron.
book-1-127.memory: Iron deficiency: warehouse empty, more trucks, little cargo.

quickCheck.question: What happens to ferritin in uncomplicated iron deficiency?

book-1-127.sourceNote: Inflammation can raise ferritin and obscure concurrent iron deficiency.

book-1-128.questionInPlainEnglish: When do severe beta-globin disorders commonly become clinically apparent?
book-1-128.explanation: Before birth and in early infancy, Hb F uses gamma chains instead of beta chains. As Hb F declines over the first months and beta-chain-dependent Hb A becomes important, a serious beta defect becomes apparent.
optionExplanations: Embryonic hemoglobins do not rely mainly on beta chains.
Newborn Hb F can temporarily mask a beta-chain defect.
Three weeks is usually too early for the full postnatal hemoglobin switch.
Around six months is the expected time for major beta-chain disorders to emerge.
book-1-128.memory: Fetal gamma protects early; beta problems show as F fades.

quickCheck.question: Why can beta-thalassemia major be less obvious at birth?
quickCheck.answer: Newborns still have abundant gamma-chain-containing Hb F.

book-1-129.questionInPlainEnglish: Which parasite-related event directly ruptures red cells during malaria?
book-1-129.explanation: Malaria parasites multiply inside red cells. When the developed merozoites break out, the host red cell ruptures. Synchronized release contributes to the classic episodes of fever and chills.
optionExplanations: Release of merozoites ruptures the infected red cell and directly causes hemolysis.
Invasion starts the red-cell infection but is not the main rupture event asked about.
Immune clearance contributes to anemia but is not the direct release-associated mechanism selected.
Parasite toxins are not the primary explanation for red-cell rupture here.
book-1-129.memory: Merozoites multiply inside, then burst out.

quickCheck.question: What happens to an infected red cell when merozoites are released?

book-1-129.sourceNote: Malaria anemia is multifactorial; immune removal and suppressed production can also contribute.

book-1-130.questionInPlainEnglish: What explains evenly spaced red-cell spicules in a severely underfilled EDTA tube?
book-1-130.explanation: Too little blood for the amount of EDTA exposes cells to excessive anticoagulant. The cells can shrink and develop regular short projections, called crenation. This is a specimen artifact rather than proof of disease.
optionExplanations: Anemia cannot be diagnosed from this storage-related shape artifact alone.
Spur cells are acanthocytes with irregular projections, not these regular crenated cells.
A dirty spreader can create artifacts, but the major clue is the extreme tube underfill.
An incorrect blood-to-anticoagulant ratio causes crenation and fits the collection history.
book-1-130.memory: Underfilled EDTA can turn cells into evenly spiked artifacts.

quickCheck.question: What is another name for a regularly spiculated crenated red cell?

book-1-131.questionInPlainEnglish: Which enzyme deficiency is the classic cause of inadequate ATP in red cells?
book-1-131.explanation: Pyruvate kinase participates in glycolysis, the red cell’s main ATP-producing pathway. Without enough ATP, membrane pumps and flexibility fail, shortening red-cell survival.
optionExplanations: Pyruvate kinase deficiency directly reduces glycolytic ATP and is the classic intended answer.
G6PD deficiency mainly weakens NADPH-dependent antioxidant protection.
Lipoprotein deficiency changes membrane lipids rather than primarily blocking ATP production.
Hexokinase also participates in glycolysis and its deficiency can reduce ATP; this is a real competing answer.
book-1-131.memory: PK powers the red-cell pump through ATP production.

quickCheck.question: Why does low ATP harm a red-cell membrane?
quickCheck.answer: Ion pumps and membrane maintenance need ATP.

book-1-131.sourceNote: This item is not fully exclusive: hexokinase deficiency can also impair glycolytic ATP generation. The book selects pyruvate kinase deficiency, the classic and more common association.

book-1-132.questionInPlainEnglish: What happens FIRST when the body uses more iron than it absorbs?
book-1-132.explanation: The body initially draws on stored iron to keep hemoglobin production going. Stores therefore shrink before hemoglobin falls enough to cause anemia. Ferritin can reveal this early depletion.
optionExplanations: Hemoglobin decreases later, after reserves and available iron become inadequate.
Iron-store depletion is the earliest change and the correct answer.
Transferrin often increases later as the body responds to iron scarcity.
The body has little ability to regulate iron by reducing excretion, so this is not the first compensatory step.
book-1-132.memory: Iron deficiency empties the warehouse before it lowers hemoglobin.

quickCheck.question: Which blood marker often falls early as iron stores decline?

book-1-133.questionInPlainEnglish: What main mechanism causes anemia during chronic inflammation?
book-1-133.explanation: Inflammation raises hepcidin, a liver-made hormone. Hepcidin closes the main iron-export route, trapping iron in storage cells and reducing intestinal absorption. Marrow cannot access enough iron even when the body has reserves.
optionExplanations: High hepcidin blocks release of stored iron and is the main mechanism listed.
Stem-cell destruction describes other marrow-failure processes, not typical inflammatory anemia.
Red-cell autoantibodies cause immune hemolysis rather than the usual mechanism here.
The erythropoietin response is blunted, not increased enough to explain the anemia.
book-1-133.memory: Hepcidin hides iron inside storage cells.

quickCheck.question: Does anemia of inflammation always mean total body iron is depleted?
quickCheck.answer: No; stored iron may be present but unavailable.

book-1-134.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement does NOT fit the book’s primary acquired sideroblastic anemia?
book-1-134.explanation: The book describes a persistent marrow disorder with ring sideroblasts, meaning iron-loaded mitochondria surround precursor nuclei. This is not B12 deficiency, so B12 injections do not reliably reverse it.
optionExplanations: Refractory means resistant to ordinary treatment, fitting the book’s description.
An unexplained heme-synthesis block fits the older idiopathic category.
Reversal with B12 injections is the incorrect statement; B12 treats a different mechanism.
An association with myelodysplastic disease fits this primary acquired form.
book-1-134.memory: Ring sideroblast iron is not fixed by treating unrelated B12 deficiency.

quickCheck.question: Which stain shows the iron ring around a sideroblast nucleus?

book-1-134.sourceNote: Modern MDS classification uses genetic findings, including SF3B1, and current therapies are broader than the book’s older RARS terminology suggests.

book-1-135.questionInPlainEnglish: Why can severe beta-thalassemia change bone shape and cause fragile bones?
book-1-135.explanation: Severe anemia constantly signals marrow to produce more red cells. The expanding marrow factory pushes outward inside bones, thinning their walls and changing facial bone structure.
optionExplanations: Calcium disorders can weaken bones, but they are not the main thalassemia mechanism here.
Hyperplastic marrow means expanded blood-making tissue and explains the bone changes.
An immune response is not the main cause of this bone expansion.
Increased fibroclast activity is not the defining process; marrow expansion is.
book-1-135.memory: Thalassemia’s overworked marrow expands and thins bone walls.

quickCheck.question: What does marrow hyperplasia mean?
quickCheck.answer: An increase in blood-making cells and tissue.

book-1-136.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement does NOT describe cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia?
book-1-136.explanation: Cold agglutinin disease usually involves IgM antibodies, often against I antigens. They bind more strongly in cooler body regions and activate complement. IgG with Rh-related specificity is more typical of warm autoimmune hemolysis.
optionExplanations: Cold-related red-cell agglutination can cause peripheral discoloration and circulation symptoms; this fits.
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection can precede cold antibody hemolysis; this fits.
Complement injury and removal of complement-coated cells can cause the hemolysis; this fits.
IgG directed against Rh antigens describes the typical warm pattern, making it the exception.
book-1-136.memory: Cold is commonly IgM/anti-I; warm is commonly IgG.

quickCheck.question: Which antibody class is typical of cold agglutinin disease?

book-1-137.questionInPlainEnglish: Which condition is most likely to produce a high RDW?
book-1-137.explanation: RDW describes how widely red-cell sizes vary. During a sickle crisis, damaged abnormal cells mix with larger new reticulocytes, creating a broad size range and a high RDW.
optionExplanations: Sickle cell disease during crisis can mix many cell sizes and strongly increase RDW.
Thalassemia minor often produces relatively uniformly small cells, with less RDW elevation.
Aplastic anemia mainly reduces production and is not the strongest size-mixture example here.
Anemia of chronic disease often has a more uniform population than sickle crisis.
book-1-137.memory: RDW rises when old abnormal cells meet large new reticulocytes.

quickCheck.question: What does a high RDW describe?
quickCheck.answer: A wide variation in red-cell size.

book-1-137.sourceNote: RDW overlaps among diseases and cannot diagnose sickle cell disease or exclude the other conditions by itself.

book-1-139.questionInPlainEnglish: Which white-cell grouping is based on JOB rather than appearance?
book-1-139.explanation: Phagocytes defend by engulfing material, while immunocytes organize targeted immune responses. The other groupings mainly describe visible granules or nuclear shape rather than cell function.
optionExplanations: Granulocytes versus nongranulocytes classifies the presence of granules, an appearance feature.
Polymorphonuclear versus mononuclear classifies nuclear shape.
Phagocytes versus immunocytes classifies major defense functions.
Granulocytes versus lymphocytes mixes cell categories rather than stating the two functional groups.
book-1-139.memory: Function asks what cells do: engulf or direct immunity.

quickCheck.question: What does a phagocyte do?

book-1-140.questionInPlainEnglish: Which normal circulating white cell is generally the largest?
book-1-140.explanation: Monocytes are large cells, often with folded nuclei and abundant gray-blue cytoplasm. They are usually larger than circulating neutrophils, eosinophils, and typical small lymphocytes.
optionExplanations: Eosinophils are granulocytes but are generally smaller than monocytes.
Neutrophils are usually smaller than monocytes.
Many normal lymphocytes are small, close to red-cell size.
Monocytes are generally the largest normal white cells in peripheral blood.
book-1-140.memory: Monocytes are the big circulating cleanup cells.

quickCheck.question: What tissue cells can circulating monocytes develop into?

book-1-141.questionInPlainEnglish: How long does a granulocyte usually remain in blood before entering tissues?
book-1-141.explanation: Granulocytes use blood mainly as transportation to tissue sites. The book’s traditional estimate is less than one day in circulation before migration, rather than many days spent freely circulating.
optionExplanations: Less than one day matches the book’s usual circulating transit estimate.
Three days is longer than the traditional blood-transit estimate.
Five days is too long for the usual circulating phase in this model.
More than ten days is not the usual blood residence time for granulocytes.
book-1-141.memory: Blood is a short transit route; tissues are the work site.

quickCheck.question: Where do granulocytes perform much of their defensive work?

book-1-141.sourceNote: Granulocyte subtype, health state, and measurement method affect lifespan estimates; this is the book’s traditional simplified model.

book-1-142.questionInPlainEnglish: What fraction of blood neutrophils is in the freely circulating pool?
book-1-142.explanation: About half the blood neutrophils are freely circulating and sampled by a routine count. The other half are temporarily marginated along vessel walls. Stress can move cells from the wall into flowing blood and raise the measured count.
optionExplanations: 100% ignores the marginated vessel-wall pool.
80% is above the traditional half-and-half estimate.
50% matches the approximate circulating share.
30% is below the usual simplified estimate.
book-1-142.memory: Neutrophils: half flowing, half along the wall.

quickCheck.question: Can stress raise a neutrophil count without immediately making new cells?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; demargination moves existing cells into circulation.

book-1-143.questionInPlainEnglish: Which cell is the main rapid phagocytic defender against bacteria?
book-1-143.explanation: Neutrophils are numerous, respond quickly to infection signals, and engulf bacteria. Monocytes also phagocytose, but they generally arrive later and help with longer-lasting cleanup.
optionExplanations: Neutrophils are the main rapid bacterial phagocytes and the correct answer.
Eosinophils are more associated with parasites and allergic responses.
Basophils release inflammatory mediators rather than serving as the major bacterial phagocyte.
Monocytes are strong phagocytes but are not usually the first dominant responders.
book-1-143.memory: Neutrophils are the early bacterial response team.

quickCheck.question: Which white cell often arrives after neutrophils to help clean up?

book-1-144.questionInPlainEnglish: Which growth-signal group chiefly promotes granulocyte and monocyte production?
book-1-144.explanation: Colony-stimulating factors tell marrow precursors to grow into particular white-cell families. GM-CSF supports granulocyte and monocyte production; G-CSF and M-CSF favor the individual branches.
optionExplanations: Erythropoietin mainly promotes red-cell production.
Colony-stimulating factors, particularly GM-CSF, regulate these white-cell lineages.
Interleukins can influence production but are a broader signal category than the intended main regulator.
Thrombopoietin mainly supports megakaryocytes and platelets.

quickCheck.question: What does the GM in GM-CSF stand for?

book-1-145.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed marrow cells belong to the dividing granulocyte pool?
book-1-145.explanation: The mitotic pool contains cells still able to divide: myeloblasts, promyelocytes, and myelocytes. Metamyelocytes and later stages no longer divide and belong to the postmitotic pool.
optionExplanations: Myeloblasts and promyelocytes are both dividing stages, so this pair fits.
Bands and segmented neutrophils are mature, nondividing stages.
Most marrow granulocytes are in the larger nondividing reserve, not the mitotic pool.
Myelocytes can divide, but metamyelocytes cannot, so the pair is mixed.
book-1-145.memory: Myelocyte is the last granulocyte stage that divides.

quickCheck.question: Can a metamyelocyte normally undergo mitosis?

book-1-146.questionInPlainEnglish: What does a left shift in circulating white cells mean?
book-1-146.explanation: A left shift means more immature neutrophil-line cells, such as bands, appear in blood. During strong demand, marrow releases younger cells from its reserve before their usual time.
optionExplanations: Redistribution from vessel walls can raise counts without increasing immature forms.
Release of more immature marrow cells into blood is a left shift.
A maturation gap is a hiatus, not a left shift.
A high lymphocyte percentage is relative lymphocytosis, not a neutrophil left shift.
book-1-146.memory: Left shift means younger neutrophils leave marrow early.

quickCheck.question: Which common immature neutrophil form often increases in a left shift?

book-1-147.explanation: Agranulocytosis means a profound shortage of granulocytes, especially neutrophils. It describes how few cells there are, not whether individual neutrophils contain visible granules.
optionExplanations: Neutrophils lacking visible granules are hypogranular; that is a morphology description.
Low granulocytes, red cells, and platelets together is pancytopenia.
Immature granulocytes in blood describe a left shift.
Markedly decreased granulocyte numbers define agranulocytosis.
book-1-147.memory: Agranulocytosis means absent or extremely few granulocytes.

quickCheck.question: Why does agranulocytosis increase infection risk?
quickCheck.answer: It removes much of the neutrophil defense against microbes.

book-1-148.questionInPlainEnglish: Which action is NOT a normal T-lymphocyte function?
book-1-148.explanation: T cells guide immune responses through signals and direct cell interactions. Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells, which develop from B lymphocytes, not by T lymphocytes.
optionExplanations: T cells secrete cytokines that coordinate immune responses; this is true.
Antibody synthesis belongs to B-cell-derived plasma cells, making this the exception.
T cells normally make up most circulating lymphocytes; this is true.
T cells regulate immune responses through helper and regulatory functions; this is true.
book-1-148.memory: T cells tell; B-derived plasma cells build antibodies.

quickCheck.question: Which cell type directly secretes large amounts of antibody?

book-1-149.questionInPlainEnglish: Is a 65% lymphocyte differential a true increase in lymphocyte number when total WBC is 4.0?
book-1-149.explanation: Multiply total WBC by the fraction: 4.0 × 0.65 = 2.6 × 10^9/L. That absolute count is within the stated range. The percentage is high only because lymphocytes make up a larger share of the available cells.
optionExplanations: 65% is above the usual adult lymphocyte percentage, so calling it normal is incorrect.
The absolute count is 2.6, not above the stated upper limit of 4.0.
Relative lymphocytosis means a high percentage with a normal absolute count; this fits.
Both cannot be present because the absolute count is normal.
book-1-149.memory: Absolute count = total count × decimal fraction.

quickCheck.question: What is the absolute lymphocyte count for WBC 4.0 and lymphocytes 65%?

book-1-150.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about white-cell inclusions or nuclear changes is correct?
book-1-150.explanation: Auer rods are needle-like collections of fused primary granules in abnormal myeloid cells. Recognizing them helps establish myeloid differentiation, especially in acute myeloid leukemia.
optionExplanations: Four lobes can be normal; hypersegmentation involves excessive lobing, not merely four.
Auer rods are fused primary granules, so this statement is correct.
Toxic granules are prominent primary azurophilic granules rather than secondary granules.
Döhle bodies contain ribosomal RNA, not patches of DNA.
book-1-150.memory: Auer rods are primary granules packed into a rod.

quickCheck.question: What material forms Döhle bodies?

book-1-150.sourceNote: Hypersegmentation is usually defined by any neutrophil with six or more lobes or an excessive proportion with five; the source’s wording is simplified.

book-86-1.questionInPlainEnglish: Which missing vitamin weakens collagen and causes scurvy-related bleeding?
book-86-1.explanation: Vitamin C helps enzymes build strong collagen, the supporting material around small blood vessels. Without it, fragile vessels leak easily, causing bruising and mucosal bleeding even when clotting factors are present.
optionExplanations: Vitamin C deficiency causes defective collagen and scurvy.
Prothrombin is clotting factor II, not the vitamin needed for collagen synthesis.
Vitamin K supports certain clotting proteins, not the collagen defect of scurvy.
Protein C regulates clotting and is not the collagen-synthesis cofactor.
book-86-1.memory: C is for Collagen and Capillary strength.

quickCheck.question: Why can scurvy cause bleeding with normal clotting-factor production?
quickCheck.answer: Weak collagen makes small blood vessels fragile.

book-86-2.questionInPlainEnglish: About how many platelets can one average megakaryocyte release?
book-86-2.explanation: A megakaryocyte is a giant marrow cell whose cytoplasm breaks into many small platelet fragments. Its size allows one cell to produce roughly 2,000–4,000 platelets.
optionExplanations: 25–50 is far below the output of one megakaryocyte.
50–200 still greatly underestimates the platelet yield.
200–500 remains below the book’s typical estimate.
2,000–4,000 matches the usual approximate yield.
book-86-2.memory: One giant megakaryocyte makes thousands of tiny platelets.

quickCheck.question: Do platelets arise as whole nucleated daughter cells?

book-86-3.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed change is NOT a usual cause of a low platelet count?
book-86-3.explanation: Thrombopoietin stimulates platelet production. Increasing that signal tends to support more platelets, whereas trapping platelets in an enlarged spleen or damaging marrow can lower the count.
optionExplanations: Splenomegaly can trap more platelets and lower the circulating count.
Chemotherapy can suppress platelet production by injuring marrow precursors.
Increased thrombopoietin stimulates production, making it the exception.
Aplastic anemia reduces marrow production of platelets and other blood cells.
book-86-3.memory: Thrombopoietin promotes platelets; marrow injury and splenic trapping reduce them.

quickCheck.question: What does thrombocytopenia mean?

book-86-4.questionInPlainEnglish: What is the term for platelets sticking to other platelets?
book-86-4.explanation: Aggregation builds a platelet clump as platelets join one another. Adhesion is the earlier attachment of platelets to an injured vessel surface rather than to another platelet.
optionExplanations: Adhesion means sticking to a vessel or another nonplatelet surface.
Aggregation means platelet-to-platelet attachment and is correct.
Release means secretion of granule contents.
Retraction means pulling the clot tighter after it forms.
book-86-4.memory: Adhesion attaches to injury; aggregation adds platelets.

quickCheck.question: What term describes platelets sticking to exposed vessel collagen?

book-86-5.questionInPlainEnglish: What directly causes the second wave in a two-phase platelet aggregation response?
book-86-5.explanation: The first stimulus activates platelets. They then release stored ADP from dense granules, recruiting and activating more platelets. This amplification creates the second aggregation wave.
optionExplanations: Fibrin formation belongs mainly to the coagulation phase, not the direct second platelet wave.
Shape change is an early activation event rather than the main second-wave signal.
Released platelet ADP triggers additional aggregation and explains the second wave.
Platelet phospholipid exposure supports coagulation but is not the direct second-wave mediator.
book-86-5.memory: Second wave comes from Stored ADP.

quickCheck.question: Which platelet granules store the ADP used to amplify aggregation?

book-86-6.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed agonist commonly produces a two-wave platelet aggregation curve?
book-86-6.explanation: At suitable concentrations, epinephrine can produce an initial response followed by a secretion-dependent second wave. The second wave reflects amplification after activated platelets release stored mediators.
optionExplanations: Arachidonic acid usually gives a strong single aggregation wave.
Collagen commonly has a lag followed by a single major response.
Epinephrine characteristically produces a biphasic response under suitable test conditions.
Ristocetin primarily tests vWF-dependent platelet agglutination rather than this classic two-wave response.
book-86-6.memory: Epinephrine can echo: first wave, then release-driven second wave.

quickCheck.question: What platelet secretion helps create epinephrine’s second wave?

book-86-6.sourceNote: Curve shape depends on agonist concentration, preparation, and laboratory method.

book-86-9.questionInPlainEnglish: Which pair of medicines mainly prevents platelets from working together?
book-86-9.explanation: Aspirin reduces platelet thromboxane production, and clopidogrel blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor. Both limit platelet activation and aggregation, whereas anticoagulants mainly target clotting proteins.
optionExplanations: Aspirin and Plavix, or clopidogrel, are antiplatelet drugs.
Warfarin and heparin are anticoagulants acting on clotting proteins.
Heparin is an anticoagulant, and protamine neutralizes heparin.
tPA and streptokinase promote clot breakdown through plasmin generation.
book-86-9.memory: Aspirin blocks thromboxane; clopidogrel blocks ADP signaling.

quickCheck.question: Which platelet receptor does clopidogrel inhibit?

book-86-9.sourceNote: The original rationale incorrectly says clopidogrel directly blocks GP IIb/IIIa. Its direct target is P2Y12; downstream GP IIb/IIIa activation is reduced.

book-86-10.questionInPlainEnglish: Which endothelial product strongly discourages platelet aggregation?
book-86-10.explanation: Healthy vessel-lining cells release prostacyclin, also called PGI2. It raises inhibitory signaling within platelets and helps keep them from clumping on an intact vessel wall.
optionExplanations: Epinephrine can stimulate platelets rather than inhibit them.
Prostacyclin is an endothelial inhibitor of platelet aggregation.
Ristocetin is a laboratory reagent that promotes vWF-dependent agglutination.
Thromboxane A2 is made by activated platelets and promotes aggregation.
book-86-10.memory: PGI2 puts platelets at peace; TXA2 turns them on.

quickCheck.question: Does thromboxane A2 promote or inhibit platelet aggregation?

book-86-11.questionInPlainEnglish: Which range best represents the book’s normal average platelet size?
book-86-11.explanation: MPV means mean platelet volume, the average size of circulating platelets. The book uses about 8–10 femtoliters; a femtoliter is a tiny unit of volume.
optionExplanations: 2–4 fL is too small for the book’s normal mean.
5–7 fL is below the selected reference estimate.
8–10 fL matches the book’s approximate normal MPV.
11–14 fL is larger than this book’s reference range.
book-86-11.memory: MPV is platelet size, just as MCV is red-cell size.

quickCheck.question: What does the M in MPV stand for?

book-86-11.sourceNote: MPV reference intervals vary with analyzer, method, anticoagulant, and time after collection.

book-86-12.questionInPlainEnglish: What does platelet distribution width measure?
book-86-12.explanation: PDW describes how varied platelet sizes are. If platelets are all similar, the distribution is narrow; if many small and large platelets are mixed, it is wider.
optionExplanations: Average platelet volume is MPV, not PDW.
Weight versus density is not what this analyzer parameter reports.
Adhesion capacity is platelet function, not a size-distribution measurement.
Variation in platelet size is the meaning of PDW.
book-86-12.memory: PDW is platelet size spread; MPV is platelet size average.

quickCheck.question: Can two samples share the same MPV but have different PDWs?
quickCheck.answer: Yes; their averages may match while their size variation differs.

book-86-13.questionInPlainEnglish: What shape does a normal platelet-size histogram usually have?
book-86-13.explanation: Most platelets cluster in the smaller-size range, with fewer large platelets. On a graph of size versus number, this makes one peak with a tail stretching right toward larger sizes.
optionExplanations: Two peaks would suggest two distinct size groups rather than the usual single population.
A left tail would point toward unusually small sizes, not the normal larger-size tail.
A single right-skewed peak describes the usual platelet histogram.
A symmetric bell shape misses the normal tail toward larger platelets.
book-86-13.memory: Normal platelet histogram: one hill, tail toward bigger cells on the right.

quickCheck.question: Which side contains the tail of a right-skewed platelet histogram?

book-86-14.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed cell is NOT a normal stage in platelet-producing cell maturation?
book-86-14.explanation: Normal development proceeds through megakaryoblast, promegakaryocyte, and mature megakaryocyte stages. Micromegakaryocytes are abnormally small megakaryocytes associated with disordered marrow development rather than a normal stage.
optionExplanations: Megakaryoblast is the earliest recognizable normal precursor.
Promegakaryocyte is an intermediate normal developmental stage.
Micromegakaryocyte is an abnormal small form, making it the exception.
Megakaryocyte is the mature platelet-producing cell.
book-86-14.memory: Micro-megakaryocyte is an abnormally small giant-cell lineage member.

quickCheck.question: What mature marrow cell releases platelets?

book-86-15.questionInPlainEnglish: Which microscope method best helps distinguish platelets from debris during a manual count?
book-86-15.explanation: Phase-contrast microscopy makes transparent, unstained particles easier to see. This helps the examiner recognize platelets in a counting chamber and avoid counting bits of debris as platelets.
optionExplanations: Electron microscopy is far too complex for a routine manual platelet count.
Dark-field microscopy is not the recommended routine method here.
Ordinary light microscopy can be used but gives less reliable contrast between platelets and debris.
Phase contrast improves discrimination and is the preferred listed method.
book-86-15.memory: Phase contrast gives pale platelets clearer outlines.

quickCheck.question: Why can debris cause an error in a manual platelet count?
quickCheck.answer: It can be mistaken for platelets.

book-86-16.questionInPlainEnglish: Calculate the platelet count and choose the result written in SI units.
book-86-16.explanation: The dilution is 1:100 because 0.02 mL blood is in 2.00 mL total. Two 1-mm² squares at 0.1-mm depth hold 0.2 µL. Thus 356 × 100 ÷ 0.2 = 178,000/µL, or 178 × 10^9/L.
optionExplanations: 178 × 10^9/L is the correct count in SI units.
178 × 10^3/µL is numerically equivalent but is not the requested SI expression.
356 × 10^9/L fails to account correctly for the two-square counting volume.
712 × 10^9/L is too high and does not follow the dilution-volume calculation.
book-86-16.memory: Count × dilution ÷ counted volume gives cells per microliter.

quickCheck.question: What is the dilution when 20 µL blood is added to 1.98 mL diluent?

book-86-17.questionInPlainEnglish: Which particle-size window traditionally identifies platelets by electrical impedance?
book-86-17.explanation: Impedance analyzers estimate particle size from electrical pulses. A typical platelet gate accepts particles around 2–20 fL, helping separate platelets from much larger red cells and very small debris.
optionExplanations: 0–10 fL would include tiny debris and miss larger platelets.
2–20 fL is the traditional platelet size gate.
15–40 fL misses most normal small platelets and includes larger particles.
35–90 fL overlaps red-cell-sized particles rather than normal platelets.
book-86-17.memory: Platelet gate is roughly two to twenty femtoliters.

quickCheck.question: Why can giant platelets be missed by an impedance platelet count?
quickCheck.answer: They may fall above the platelet size gate.

book-86-17.sourceNote: Actual analyzer gates and classification methods vary; optical and fluorescence methods use additional information.

book-86-18.questionInPlainEnglish: Which stored substance is commonly deficient in platelet storage-pool disease?
book-86-18.explanation: Dense platelet granules store ADP, which is released to call more platelets into an aggregate. In dense-granule storage-pool disease, too little stored ADP weakens that recruitment signal.
optionExplanations: ADP is stored in dense granules and is the intended deficiency.
PF3 refers to the platelet phospholipid surface, not the missing dense-granule cargo.
Thrombasthenin is a contractile protein term, not the main stored signaling substance here.
Thromboxane A2 is synthesized after activation rather than stored as the key dense-granule cargo.
book-86-18.memory: Dense granules store ADP for the next aggregation wave.

quickCheck.question: What aggregation feature can be weak when platelet ADP release is deficient?

book-86-18.sourceNote: Storage-pool disorders include different granule defects; the question specifically describes dense-granule deficiency.

book-86-19.questionInPlainEnglish: Which anticoagulant is used for routine PT and aPTT collection?
book-86-19.explanation: Sodium citrate temporarily binds calcium, preventing clotting during collection. The laboratory then adds a controlled amount of calcium to begin testing. Correct tube fill preserves the required blood-to-citrate ratio.
optionExplanations: Heparin directly inhibits clotting reactions and interferes with routine clot-time assays.
Sodium citrate is the standard anticoagulant for routine coagulation testing.
Acid citrate dextrose is used for other purposes and is not the routine coagulation tube additive.
Sodium fluoride mainly inhibits glycolysis for glucose-related testing.
book-86-19.memory: Citrate catches calcium; the test adds calcium back.

quickCheck.question: What usual blood-to-citrate ratio is required?
quickCheck.answer: Nine parts blood to one part citrate.

book-86-20.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed protein is chiefly produced outside liver parenchymal cells?
book-86-20.explanation: Von Willebrand factor is made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. It helps platelets attach to injured vessels and carries factor VIII. The book contrasts this with proteins commonly grouped as liver-produced.
optionExplanations: Factor VIII is associated with hepatic production, but its major source is endothelial cells, especially liver sinusoidal endothelium.
Plasminogen is synthesized in the liver.
Protein C is synthesized in the liver.
Von Willebrand factor is made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes and is the book’s exception.
book-86-20.memory: vWF comes from vessel-lining cells and platelet-making cells.

quickCheck.question: Which two cell types make von Willebrand factor?

book-86-20.sourceNote: The liver-versus-endothelium distinction is oversimplified: factor VIII is mainly made by endothelial cells, including liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, rather than hepatocytes. The book’s answer remains vWF.

book-86-22.questionInPlainEnglish: Which two clotting-factor deficiencies classically follow X-linked recessive inheritance?
book-86-22.explanation: Hemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency and hemophilia B is factor IX deficiency. Both usually follow X-linked inheritance, so males with the altered gene are commonly affected.
optionExplanations: Factor VIII fits, but factor V deficiency is usually autosomal rather than X-linked.
Factors VIII and IX are the classic X-linked hemophilia factors.
Factor IX fits, but factor X deficiency is usually autosomal.
vWF disorders are generally autosomal, so this pair is not the X-linked pair.
book-86-22.memory: A is eight; B is nine.

quickCheck.question: Which factor is deficient in hemophilia B, also called Christmas disease?

book-86-23.questionInPlainEnglish: Which association does the book select for prekallikrein deficiency?
book-86-23.explanation: Prekallikrein helps start contact activation in an aPTT tube. Its deficiency can greatly prolong aPTT, yet usually causes no abnormal bleeding. The book links it to thrombosis through reduced fibrinolysis, but that risk claim is not firmly established.
optionExplanations: A factor deficiency usually corrects with normal-plasma mixing, so noncorrection is not expected.
Prekallikrein deficiency is usually autosomal recessive, not dominant.
Increased thrombosis risk is the book’s selected association, but evidence is uncertain.
Delayed wound bleeding is more characteristic of factor XIII deficiency.
book-86-23.memory: Prekallikrein deficiency can make aPTT look alarming without causing bleeding.

quickCheck.question: Does prekallikrein deficiency usually correct in a mixing study?

book-86-23.sourceNote: The book overstates a proven thrombotic tendency. Current understanding does not establish prekallikrein deficiency alone as a definite thrombophilia.

book-86-24.questionInPlainEnglish: Which deficiency does NOT prolong thrombin time?
book-86-24.explanation: The thrombin-time test adds ready-made thrombin to plasma. This skips the need to convert prothrombin, factor II, into thrombin. The test instead depends on fibrinogen and whether thrombin can act normally.
optionExplanations: Fibrin degradation products can interfere with fibrin formation and prolong the test.
Heparin inhibits the added thrombin and can prolong the test.
Factor I is fibrinogen; too little fibrinogen prolongs clot formation.
Factor II deficiency is bypassed by adding thrombin, so it does not itself prolong thrombin time.
book-86-24.memory: Thrombin time supplies IIa, so it bypasses II.

quickCheck.question: Which factor is fibrinogen?

book-86-25.questionInPlainEnglish: What PT and aPTT results are expected in factor XIII deficiency?
book-86-25.explanation: PT and aPTT stop timing when the first fibrin clot forms. Factor XIII works afterward, fastening fibrin strands together. A clot can therefore appear on time but remain unstable and cause delayed bleeding.
optionExplanations: PT is usually normal because initial fibrin formation is intact.
aPTT is usually normal for the same reason.
Both prolonged would suggest an earlier shared-pathway problem rather than isolated XIII deficiency.
Both normal is expected because neither test measures later fibrin cross-linking.
book-86-25.memory: XIII secures the clot after PT and aPTT stop the clock.

quickCheck.question: Which factor deficiency can cause delayed bleeding despite normal PT and aPTT?

book-86-25.sourceNote: Specific factor XIII activity testing is preferred; clot-solubility screening may miss milder deficiencies.

book-86-26.questionInPlainEnglish: Which test pattern best fits warfarin treatment?
book-86-26.explanation: Warfarin lowers functional vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. PT/INR rises, and aPTT may also rise because shared and intrinsic factors are affected. Warfarin does not directly lower platelet count or impair platelet function.
optionExplanations: A normal INR with platelet abnormalities does not fit typical warfarin action.
Raised PT/INR with possible raised aPTT and normal platelet measures is the best listed combination.
Completely normal clotting tests do not show the usual therapeutic effect.
The raised INR fits, but a low platelet count and prolonged bleeding time are not expected direct effects.
book-86-26.memory: Warfarin affects clotting factors, so INR rises while platelets usually stay normal.

quickCheck.question: Which test is used to monitor warfarin?

book-86-26.sourceNote: aPTT prolongation is variable and reagent-dependent; therapeutic warfarin does not always produce an abnormal aPTT.

book-86-27.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed complex is NOT essential for normal clotting inside the body?
book-86-27.explanation: Normal in-body clotting is initiated mainly by tissue factor and factor VIIa. Contact-system proteins strongly influence laboratory aPTT testing, but deficiency of factor XII, prekallikrein, or HMWK usually does not cause bleeding.
optionExplanations: VIIa with tissue factor and calcium starts coagulation in vivo.
IXa with VIIIa, calcium, and phospholipid forms the tenase complex that activates X.
Xa with Va, calcium, and phospholipid forms prothrombinase and generates thrombin.
XIIa, kallikrein, and HMWK are contact-system components that are not essential for normal bleeding control.
book-86-27.memory: Contact factors matter in the tube more than in stopping a wound.

quickCheck.question: Why can factor XII deficiency prolong aPTT without a bleeding tendency?
quickCheck.answer: The laboratory test depends on contact activation, but normal in-body clotting can start through tissue factor.

book-86-27.sourceNote: The options abbreviate active cofactors VIIIa and Va as VIII and V; PF3 means platelet phospholipid surface.

book-86-29.questionInPlainEnglish: Which enzyme ties fibrin strands together to strengthen a clot?
book-86-29.explanation: Activated factor XIII, written XIIIa, makes strong chemical cross-links between fibrin strands. Think of adding permanent fasteners after a loose net has formed.
optionExplanations: Alpha-2-antiplasmin restrains plasmin, not directly cross-linking fibrin strands.
Factor XIIIa cross-links fibrin and stabilizes the clot.
Plasmin cuts fibrin apart rather than strengthening it.
Thrombin makes fibrin and activates XIII, but XIIIa performs the actual cross-linking.
book-86-29.memory: Thrombin builds the net; XIIIa fastens the knots.

quickCheck.question: What does the “a” in XIIIa indicate?
quickCheck.answer: The activated form of factor XIII.

book-86-31.questionInPlainEnglish: Which active enzyme cuts apart a stabilized fibrin clot?
book-86-31.explanation: Plasmin digests fibrin into smaller fragments. It is formed when activators such as tPA convert inactive plasminogen into active plasmin.
optionExplanations: Plasminogen is the inactive precursor and cannot perform the digestion until activated.
Plasmin is the active fibrin-digesting enzyme.
Prothrombin is the precursor of thrombin, not the fibrin-digesting enzyme.
Thrombin helps form fibrin rather than being the main clot-dissolving enzyme.
book-86-31.memory: Plasmin pulls the fibrin net apart.

quickCheck.question: What inactive protein is converted into plasmin?

book-86-32.questionInPlainEnglish: Which general target group is associated with lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin antibodies?
book-86-32.explanation: These belong to the antiphospholipid antibody family. They interfere with phospholipid-dependent clotting tests, often prolonging aPTT, even though persistent clinically significant antibodies can be associated with thrombosis in the body.
optionExplanations: Factor V antibodies would be a specific factor inhibitor rather than the general antiphospholipid family.
Factor VIII inhibitors target a protein factor and more often cause bleeding.
Factor IX inhibitors are distinct specific factor antibodies.
Phospholipid-associated targets identify the family intended here.
book-86-32.memory: Lupus anticoagulant can slow the tube but accompany clots in the body.

quickCheck.question: Can a lupus anticoagulant be present in someone without lupus?

book-86-32.sourceNote: Many clinically important antiphospholipid antibodies recognize phospholipid-binding proteins, especially beta-2 glycoprotein I or prothrombin, rather than bare phospholipid alone.

book-86-33.explanation: Heparin greatly accelerates antithrombin’s ability to shut down activated clotting enzymes, including thrombin and factor Xa. It boosts an existing natural brake rather than preventing the liver from making factors.
optionExplanations: Binding calcium is the mechanism of citrate and EDTA, not heparin.
Reduced thrombin generation can result, but this does not state heparin’s main direct mechanism.
Producing nonfunctional vitamin K-dependent factors describes warfarin.
Enhancing antithrombin is heparin’s central mechanism.
book-86-33.memory: Heparin helps antithrombin hit the brakes.

quickCheck.question: Which natural anticoagulant does heparin amplify?

book-86-34.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed protein is a major natural inhibitor of clotting enzymes?
book-86-34.explanation: Antithrombin neutralizes several activated clotting enzymes, especially thrombin and factor Xa. It is a broad natural brake on secondary hemostasis, the fibrin-forming part of clotting.
optionExplanations: Antithrombin directly inhibits several activated enzymes and is the intended main regulator.
Protein C is another important regulator but works chiefly by disabling cofactors Va and VIIIa.
Alpha-2-antiplasmin regulates clot breakdown by inhibiting plasmin.
tPA promotes fibrin breakdown by activating plasminogen rather than directly restraining the coagulation cascade.
book-86-34.memory: Antithrombin blocks clotting enzymes; protein C switches off helpers.

quickCheck.question: Name one activated factor inhibited by antithrombin.

book-86-35.questionInPlainEnglish: Why can routine aPTT miss a deficiency of platelet clot-supporting phospholipid?
book-86-35.explanation: Routine aPTT uses platelet-poor plasma and supplies phospholipid in its reagent. That substitute provides the surface normally supplied by activated platelets, so the test does not depend on the patient’s own PF3 activity.
optionExplanations: Platelet-poor, not platelet-rich, plasma is normally used.
Reagent phospholipid replaces PF3 and masks a patient platelet-surface defect.
PF3 instability in the reagent is not the reason.
Platelet phospholipid supports these reactions in the body; the test simply supplies a substitute.
book-86-35.memory: aPTT brings its own phospholipid surface.

quickCheck.question: Does routine aPTT require the patient’s own platelets to provide PF3?

book-86-36.questionInPlainEnglish: What part of clot formation is tested when thrombin is added directly to plasma?
book-86-36.explanation: Added thrombin converts fibrinogen to fibrin. The test bypasses the upstream pathways, so it mainly evaluates the final fibrinogen-to-fibrin step rather than production of thrombin.
optionExplanations: Fibrinogen amount and function affect the time to fibrin formation, making this the intended answer.
Prothrombin is bypassed because active thrombin is already supplied.
The extrinsic pathway lies upstream and is bypassed.
The intrinsic pathway is also upstream and bypassed.
book-86-36.memory: Adding thrombin asks whether fibrinogen can become fibrin.

quickCheck.question: Is prothrombin activation needed after thrombin reagent is added?

book-86-36.sourceNote: A thrombin time is affected by fibrinogen quantity, fibrinogen function, inhibitors such as heparin, and fibrin-degradation products; it is not a specific concentration measurement by itself.

book-86-37.questionInPlainEnglish: Correct a fibrinogen value for using twice the usual dilution.
book-86-37.explanation: The standard curve assumes a 1:10 sample. A 1:20 sample is twice as dilute, so multiply the curve reading by 20/10 = 2. The reported fibrinogen is 400 × 2 = 800 mg/dL.
optionExplanations: 160 mg/dL does not use the required dilution correction.
200 mg/dL divides by two when the extra dilution requires multiplication.
400 mg/dL is the uncorrected curve reading.
800 mg/dL correctly doubles the reading for the additional dilution.
book-86-37.memory: Twice as dilute means double the curve result.

quickCheck.question: If a 1:20 result reads 300 mg/dL on a 1:10 curve, what is the corrected concentration?

book-86-38.questionInPlainEnglish: Which statement about INR is NOT true in the book’s intended sense?
book-86-38.explanation: INR adjusts PT results using the reagent’s sensitivity so warfarin monitoring is more comparable between laboratories. The book therefore rejects the claim that INR simply depends on the local reagent and instrument like raw PT seconds do.
optionExplanations: Uncorrected dependence on reagent and instrument is the statement the book labels false.
INR = PT ratio raised to ISI is the correct calculation.
INR is recommended for monitoring stable vitamin K antagonist treatment.
A common warfarin target is 2.0–3.0, with different targets for some indications.

quickCheck.question: What exponent is used in the INR calculation?
quickCheck.answer: The ISI, or international sensitivity index.

book-86-38.sourceNote: INR standardization reduces rather than completely eliminates reagent and instrument effects. The ISI should be appropriate for the reagent-instrument combination.

book-86-39.questionInPlainEnglish: Why can aPTT become prolonged during DIC even though clotting is overactive?
book-86-39.explanation: DIC starts widespread clot formation, which uses up clotting factors and platelets. The remaining plasma can become deficient in factors, so it takes longer to clot in the test tube even while dangerous clotting occurs in the body.
optionExplanations: An additional extrinsic-only defect is not needed to explain a prolonged aPTT.
DIC is not primarily production of inherently unstable factors.
Consumption faster than replacement depletes factors and explains prolonged clotting times.
Excess clotting and factor deficiency can coexist, so the diagnosis is not contradicted.
book-86-39.memory: DIC clots everywhere, then leaves too few supplies.

quickCheck.question: Why can DIC cause both thrombosis and bleeding?
quickCheck.answer: Microclots form while consuming platelets and clotting factors.

book-86-39.sourceNote: “DIG” in the source is an OCR error for DIC.

book-86-40.questionInPlainEnglish: Which result is NOT typical of DIC?
book-86-40.explanation: DIC consumes clotting factors, platelets, and natural inhibitors such as antithrombin. Clot breakdown raises D-dimer and other degradation products. Antithrombin usually falls rather than rises.
optionExplanations: Low fibrinogen can result from consumption and breakdown, fitting DIC.
Positive degradation-product testing fits widespread clot formation and lysis.
Low platelets fit consumption in microclots.
Increased antithrombin is the exception because antithrombin is usually depleted.
book-86-40.memory: DIC consumes platelets, fibrinogen, and antithrombin.

quickCheck.question: What happens to D-dimer when cross-linked clots are being broken down?

book-86-40.sourceNote: Fibrinogen may be normal or high early in inflammatory DIC; serial trends and the overall pattern matter. “DIG” is an OCR error.

book-86-42.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed disorder is the book’s main indication for aminocaproic acid?
book-86-42.explanation: Aminocaproic acid limits plasmin generation and action on fibrin, reducing excessive clot breakdown. The book selects primary fibrinogenolysis, where inappropriate fibrinolytic activity destroys fibrinogen without preceding widespread clot formation.
optionExplanations: It may help selected mucosal bleeding in vWD, but it does not replace the missing vWF.
It can be an adjunct in some hemophilia bleeding, but it does not replace factor VIII.
Blocking breakdown during active DIC can worsen persistent microclots and is not routine therapy.
Primary fibrinogenolysis is the book’s intended setting for suppressing inappropriate breakdown.
book-86-42.memory: Aminocaproic acid applies the brakes to fibrinolysis.

quickCheck.question: Which clot-dissolving system does aminocaproic acid suppress?

book-86-42.sourceNote: “Treatment of choice” is too broad: management depends on the cause and clinical setting. Antifibrinolytics also have important uses as adjuncts in other bleeding disorders.

book-86-43.questionInPlainEnglish: Which missing platelet receptor most directly impairs clot retraction?
book-86-43.explanation: Platelets use GP IIb/IIIa, also called integrin alpha-IIb beta-3, to bind fibrinogen and connect to the clot. Without this connection, platelets cannot aggregate normally or pull the fibrin network inward effectively.
optionExplanations: GP Ib mediates vWF-dependent adhesion; its deficiency causes Bernard-Soulier syndrome.
GP IIb/IIIa deficiency causes Glanzmann thrombasthenia and defective retraction.
Low dense-granule ADP impairs recruitment but does not define this classic retraction defect.
Absent vWF impairs adhesion and factor VIII carriage rather than the main fibrin-pulling connection.
book-86-43.memory: IIb/IIIa grips the clot so platelets can pull it tight.

quickCheck.question: Which inherited disorder has defective GP IIb/IIIa?

book-86-43.sourceNote: The original rationale incorrectly attributes Glanzmann retraction failure to absent actomyosin; the defining defect is GP IIb/IIIa-mediated fibrin(ogen) interaction.

book-86-44.questionInPlainEnglish: Which condition typically raises rather than lowers the platelet count?
book-86-44.explanation: Polycythemia vera is a marrow stem-cell disorder that can overproduce red cells, granulocytes, and platelets. The other options commonly lower platelets by consumption, trapping, or immune removal.
optionExplanations: DIC consumes platelets in microclots and usually lowers the count.
An enlarged spleen can sequester platelets and lower the circulating count.
Polycythemia vera can increase megakaryocyte output and cause thrombocytosis.
ITP destroys platelets through immune mechanisms and lowers the count.
book-86-44.memory: PV can turn up all three marrow production lines.

quickCheck.question: What does thrombocytosis mean?

book-86-45.questionInPlainEnglish: Which action is NOT performed by the listed vessel-lining cell products?
book-86-45.explanation: Endothelial cells help prevent unnecessary clotting using prostacyclin, tPA, and thrombomodulin. Directly cross-linking fibrin is instead the work of activated factor XIII.
optionExplanations: Prostacyclin from endothelium inhibits platelet aggregation, so this is a real endothelial role.
Endothelial tPA activates plasminogen and supports fibrinolysis.
Endothelial thrombomodulin changes thrombin’s activity toward protein C activation.
Fibrin cross-linking is performed by factor XIIIa, making this the exception.
book-86-45.memory: Endothelium restrains and clears clots; XIIIa cross-links them.

quickCheck.question: Which endothelial surface protein helps thrombin activate protein C?

book-86-45.sourceNote: Thrombomodulin is a surface-bound endothelial protein rather than simply a released product; the question groups endothelial functions loosely.

book-86-46.questionInPlainEnglish: Which listed test historically screened platelet FUNCTION rather than platelet NUMBER?
book-86-46.explanation: A qualitative defect means platelets are present but do not work properly. The book chooses bleeding time because it was used to assess primary hemostasis. It has largely been abandoned because it is poorly reproducible and does not reliably predict bleeding.
optionExplanations: Platelet count measures quantity, so it can be normal despite defective function.
PT evaluates plasma clotting factors rather than platelet function.
A 5 M urea clot-solubility test screens severe factor XIII deficiency.
Bleeding time is the historical functional screening answer among these choices.
book-86-46.memory: Quantity counts platelets; quality asks whether they work.

quickCheck.question: Can a normal platelet count exclude a platelet-function disorder?

book-86-46.sourceNote: Bleeding time is an outdated clinical test. Modern evaluation may use platelet aggregation, secretion studies, flow cytometry, or other laboratory-selected methods.

book-86-47.questionInPlainEnglish: Which set lists the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors?
book-86-47.explanation: Vitamin K helps the liver modify factors II, VII, IX, and X so they can bind calcium and work on phospholipid surfaces. Without this modification, the proteins may be present but function poorly.
optionExplanations: I, V, VIII, and XIII are not the classic vitamin K-dependent set.
II and IX fit, but V and XII do not.
II, VII, IX, and X are the complete classic clotting-factor set.
XI, XII, prekallikrein, and HMWK are not the vitamin K-dependent group.

quickCheck.question: Which vitamin is required to make functional factors II, VII, IX, and X?

book-86-48.questionInPlainEnglish: Which natural anticoagulant proteins lose function during warfarin treatment?
book-86-48.explanation: Proteins C and S require vitamin K-dependent modification, just like several procoagulant factors. Warfarin therefore reduces these natural brakes too, which helps explain the temporary clotting imbalance when treatment begins.
optionExplanations: Prothrombin is vitamin K-dependent, but fibrinogen is not.
Stable factor VII is vitamin K-dependent, but labile factor V is not.
Both protein C and protein S are vitamin K-dependent and are reduced by warfarin.
Fletcher and Fitzgerald are contact proteins that do not depend on vitamin K.
book-86-48.memory: Vitamin K supports brakes C and S as well as factors 2, 7, 9, 10.

quickCheck.question: Why can starting warfarin briefly reduce natural anticoagulant protection?
quickCheck.answer: Protein C can fall before longer-lived procoagulant factors have declined.

book-86-49.questionInPlainEnglish: Which paired choice does the book consider the EXCEPTION among clot-risk conditions?
book-86-49.explanation: The book chooses the pair containing hypofibrinogenemia because too little fibrinogen is classically linked to bleeding. However, the other member, hyperhomocysteinemia, is associated with thrombosis, so the option is poorly constructed.
optionExplanations: Factor V Leiden resists protein C, and prothrombin G20210A can raise prothrombin; both are clot-risk variants.
Hypofibrinogenemia is the book’s exception, but hyperhomocysteinemia in the same option does carry a clot association.
Persistent clinically significant lupus anticoagulant or anticardiolipin antibodies can accompany thrombosis.
Antithrombin and protein C deficiencies remove natural clotting brakes and increase venous thrombosis risk.
book-86-49.memory: Missing anticoagulant brakes promotes clots; low fibrinogen classically suggests bleeding.

quickCheck.question: What is the functional effect of factor V Leiden?
quickCheck.answer: Activated factor V becomes resistant to inactivation by activated protein C.

book-86-49.sourceNote: The chosen pair mixes a bleeding-associated disorder with a clot-associated condition. Thrombosis can also occur in congenital fibrinogen disorders. The source also incorrectly implies G20210A makes a structurally abnormal prothrombin; it usually increases prothrombin levels.

book-86-50.questionInPlainEnglish: Which diagnosis and clot-dissolving drug match sudden speech difficulty and one-sided paralysis?
book-86-50.explanation: These focal neurologic symptoms suggest stroke. If imaging confirms an eligible acute ischemic stroke, a thrombolytic such as tPA can promote plasmin formation and dissolve the obstructing clot. D-dimer alone cannot establish the diagnosis or treatment eligibility.
optionExplanations: Myocardial infarction usually presents with cardiac symptoms; aspirin is antiplatelet rather than a clot-dissolving drug.
Pulmonary embolism causes lung-related symptoms, and warfarin does not dissolve an existing clot directly.
DVT causes limb symptoms, and heparin prevents extension rather than directly lysing the clot.
Stroke best fits the neurologic symptoms; tPA is the listed fibrinolytic treatment when the patient is eligible.
book-86-50.memory: One-sided weakness plus speech trouble points to brain ischemia; tPA activates plasmin.

quickCheck.question: What must be excluded by brain imaging before stroke thrombolysis?

book-86-50.sourceNote: The stem’s D-dimer-driven immediate treatment is misleading. Acute stroke requires urgent imaging and formal time-window/eligibility assessment; elevated D-dimer is nonspecific and is not a prerequisite for thrombolysis.

book-86-51.questionInPlainEnglish: Which medicine can reverse an overdose of unfractionated heparin?
book-86-51.explanation: Protamine is positively charged and binds negatively charged heparin, neutralizing its anticoagulant effect. Dosing depends on the heparin dose and time since administration.
optionExplanations: Vitamin K reverses vitamin K antagonist effects, not heparin.
Protamine sulfate binds and neutralizes unfractionated heparin.
Antithrombin would support heparin’s anticoagulant action rather than reverse it.
Warfarin is another anticoagulant, not a heparin antidote.
book-86-51.memory: Protamine pairs with heparin; vitamin K counters warfarin.

quickCheck.question: What is the usual reversal agent for unfractionated heparin?

book-86-52.questionInPlainEnglish: Which description correctly identifies protein C?
book-86-52.explanation: Protein C is a liver-produced, vitamin K-dependent natural anticoagulant. Once activated, it works with protein S to inactivate factors Va and VIIIa, reducing further thrombin production.
optionExplanations: A vitamin K-dependent inhibitor of clotting accurately describes protein C.
Protein C inactivates Va and VIIIa rather than activating them.
Protein C’s defining role is limiting coagulation, not serving as the main inhibitor of fibrinolysis.
